title: I am with you always (Matthew 28:16–20)
hookLine: on a mountain in Galilee, some worshiped, some doubted; go, make disciples
carry: to the end of the age
tomorrow: Acts opens with a goodbye. why are his last orders 'wait'?

lines: THEY WORSHIPPED HIM: BUT SOME DOUBTED.
HE CAME AND SPAKE UNTO THEM.
cards: End-of-trip group photos usually get a caption like best week ever. Matthew's last group photo has a strange one.

The eleven go to a mountain in Galilee, they see the risen Jesus, and the King James says: "And when they saw him, they worshipped him: but some doubted." Some doubted. On the last page, standing right there.
So what does Jesus do with the doubters? Matthew's next words: "And Jesus came and spake unto them." He comes closer, and speaks to all of them.

teach.b: Here's the puzzle: why keep the doubt in? Matthew could have ended on a crowd of the certain.

teach.h: GO YE THEREFORE, ALL OF YOU.
teach.b: Instead the sending goes to the whole mixed group: "Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost."
Nobody is sorted first into the sure and the unsure. Then the last line of the book: "and, lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world."
The King James says the end of the world; some translations say the end of the age, which is where today's line comes from. One to tell a friend: Matthew starts and ends on the same promise.
On his first page the child is to be called Emmanuel, "which being interpreted is, God with us."

teach.h: I AM WITH YOU, LAST PAGE.
teach.b: On his last, I am with you. In between, these lessons read Matthew through: a family tree with hard names, a sower, five loaves, seventy times seven, a table, a garden, a cross, a sealed stone, two women running.

teach.h: TO THE END OF THE AGE.
teach.b: So the answer to the puzzle: Matthew doesn't solve the doubt. He answers it with a presence. Not proof first and company later, but company that comes closer, to the worshipers and the doubters alike, and stays.

how: Some churches read Matthew 28:16–20 at baptisms, where the words of 28:19 are often spoken over the person being baptized.

games.q: what does “i am with you always” mean?
o: a farewell meaning I'll be gone for a while
a promise of presence, all the way to the end
a vow to come back on one fixed future day

games.q: the last page — tap the pairs.
p: God with us, on the first page
even unto the end of the world

s: everyone on the mountain was certain by the end
they worshipped him: but some doubted. Matthew keeps the doubt on his last page.
Jesus comes closer to speak to them
and Jesus came and spake unto them, to the whole group.
the King James ends Matthew with 'the end of the age'
it says 'even unto the end of the world'; some newer translations say age.

games.q: your friend moves across the country next week. late at night she admits she isn't sure about anything right now, God included. what fits Matthew's last page?
o: promise you'll keep showing up for her, doubts and all.
tell her to settle her doubts before the big move.
change the subject until she sounds sure again.
games.why: Matthew sends worshipers and doubters out together, and the last word is a promise of presence, not a demand for certainty.

practice: Hold one thing you'll carry all day: keys, a phone, a ring. Let it stand for one doubt you'll bring along today, unsolved.
Then, breathing slowly, let the same small object stand for the promise too, so the doubt and the promise travel in the same pocket.

wordCard.voice: I am with you always. The last words of Matthew's Gospel, spoken on a mountain to people who worshiped and doubted.

orig.note: Greek: of the age. Matthew 28:20 ends at the completion of the age, which the KJV renders the end of the world.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: to the end of the age, with the doubters included. Matthew, read through.
